messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Malia was 67 years old, a widow of twelve years, and a database administrator for a mid-sized logistics firm in Honolulu. She had spent decades organizing information into clean, logical structures, and she had taken pride in that. But for the past three years, since the end of a relationship she had entered late in life with a man named Keone, the internal architecture of her mind had felt like a corrupted file—fragmented, unreliable, and alien. The trauma itself had not been a single catastrophic blow but a slow, grinding campaign of physical abuse that escalated over eighteen months. The worst moment, the one that now surfaced without warning, had happened in her own kitchen. Keone had accused her of hiding his phone. She had not. He had grabbed her by the wrist, twisting until she felt the bones grind, and then he had shoved her backward into the counter, the edge catching her just below the ribs. She had crumpled to the tile floor, gasping, and he had stood over her and said, “See what you make me do.” The words had lodged in her chest like shrapnel.

In the months after she finally left him, Malia had not told anyone the full story. She had not filed a police report. She had told herself it was over, that she could simply move on. But moving on had not happened. Instead, she had begun to notice that she could no longer look people in the eye. At work, when her younger colleague, Noah, leaned into her cubicle to ask a question, she would fix her gaze on her monitor or on a spot on the wall just past his shoulder. She knew this made her seem cold or evasive, and she hated that, but whenever she tried to meet someone’s eyes, she felt a flash of the same helpless exposure she had felt staring up at Keone from the kitchen floor. She had come to believe that her reactions since the event proved she was a lousy coper—that other women, stronger women, would have handled it differently, would have been able to look people in the eye and get on with their lives. Instead, she felt defective, as though something fundamental was wrong with her as a person.

She had also started avoiding physical contact. When a friend reached out to touch her arm in sympathy during a conversation about her husband’s death years earlier, Malia had flinched so sharply that the friend had pulled back, hurt and confused. Malia had apologized, but she had not explained. The sensation of an unexpected hand on her skin sent a jolt through her that was not exactly pain but something worse—a visceral certainty that her body was no longer her own. She began to sit with her purse in her lap on the bus, creating a barrier. She chose the end seat in meetings so that no one could sit beside her. Her social world, already narrowed by widowhood, contracted further.

Sleep had become a battleground. She stayed up until two or three in the morning, watching old cooking shows, because the moment she closed her eyes, the kitchen scene replayed itself with merciless clarity. She could feel the cold tile against her cheek, hear Keone’s breathing, taste the metallic edge of fear. So she delayed sleep, night after night, until exhaustion forced her into a shallow, restless unconsciousness. The consequences accumulated. She was late to work twice in one week, something that had never happened in her thirty-year career. Her supervisor, a patient man named James, asked gently if everything was all right. Malia had said she was having trouble sleeping, and he had nodded and suggested she see a doctor. She had nodded back, but she had not gone.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the grocery store. A man in the aisle—broad-shouldered, wearing a baseball cap, with a certain set to his jaw—had reached past her for a can of beans, and for a split second, her vision had tunneled. Her heart had slammed against her ribs, and she had dropped her shopping basket, cans rolling across the linoleum. She had stood there, trembling, while strangers stared. That night, alone in her apartment, she had looked at herself in the bathroom mirror and not recognized the woman staring back. She felt like she did not know herself anymore. The next morning, she had called a therapist’s office. She was terrified that talking about it would make it worse, that she would be confirming once and for all that she was broken. But she was also terrified of spending the rest of her life flinching at shadows. She did not know if she could be fixed. She only knew she could not go on like this.
